title: How much activity, and what do you get?
goal: State the WHO weekly activity target in MET-minutes, describe the shape of the activity–mortality curve, and judge what cohort data on steps and device-measured activity can and cannot show.

steps.title: What the guidelines ask for
steps.text:
The WHO 2020 guidelines ask every adult for **150–300 min of moderate** or **75–150 min of vigorous** aerobic activity a week, or an equal mix [[c:who-dose]]. They add muscle-strengthening work and less sitting, and say that some activity beats none and more is better [[c:who-more]].

To compare mixed weeks, count in [METs](g:met). Resting is 1 MET, about 3.5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ of oxygen [[c:met-def]]; moderate effort is 3 to under 6 METs, vigorous 6 or more [[c:met-bands]]. **MET-minutes** = minutes × METs. Divide by 60 for [MET-hours](g:met-hours). The minimum of 150 min at 3 METs is 450 MET-min, or 7.5 MET-h [[c:min-met]].

claims.text: WHO 2020: adults should do 150–300 min of moderate or 75–150 min of vigorous aerobic activity a week, or an equivalent mix.

evidence.quote: All adults should undertake 150-300 min of moderate-intensity, or 75-150 min of vigorous-intensity physical activity, or some equivalent combination of moderate-intensity and vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity, per week.

claims.text: The WHO guidelines state that some activity is better than none and that more is better for health outcomes.

evidence.quote: They reaffirm messages that some physical activity is better than none, that more physical activity is better for optimal health outcomes and provide a new recommendation on reducing sedentary behaviours.

claims.text: One MET is the oxygen used sitting at rest, set by convention at 3.5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹.

evidence.quote: One metabolic equivalent (MET) is defined as the amount of oxygen consumed while sitting at rest and is equal to 3.5 ml O2 per kg body weight x min.

claims.text: WHO defines moderate intensity as 3 to under 6 METs and vigorous as 6 METs or more.

evidence.quote: On an absolute scale, moderate-intensity refers to the physical activity that is performed between 3 and <6 times the intensity of rest (METs).
On an absolute scale, vigorous intensity refers to physical activity that is performed at 6.0 or more METs.

claims.text: The guideline minimum of 75 vigorous or 150 moderate minutes a week equals 7.5 MET-hours a week.

evidence.quote: The 2008 Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans recommended a minimum of 75 vigorous-intensity or 150 moderate-intensity minutes per week (7.5 metabolic-equivalent hours per week) of aerobic activity for substantial health benefit

steps.title: Counting a week in MET-minutes
steps.problem: A runner does 3 runs of 40 min at 9 METs and 1 walk of 45 min at 3 METs. How many MET-minutes is that, and how does it compare with the 450 MET-min minimum?
steps: Group the minutes by effort: runs 3 × 40 = 120 min at 9 METs; walk 45 min at 3 METs.
MET-min = minutes × METs: 120 × 9 = 1,080 and 45 × 3 = 135. Total 1,215 MET-min.
Compare: 1,215 ÷ 450 = 2.7, so this week is 2.7 times the minimum.

steps.title: The curve is steep at first, then flat
steps.text:
Arem pooled six US and European [cohorts](g:cohort-study): 661,137 adults and 116,686 deaths over a median 14.2 years [[c:arem-curve]]. Leisure activity is shown in multiples of the minimum (7.5 MET-h·week⁻¹), against doing none:

| activity | hazard ratio for death |
|---|---|
| under 1× | 0.80 |
| 1–2× | 0.69 |
| 2–3× | 0.63 |
| 3–5× | 0.61 |
| 10× or more | 0.69 |

A [hazard ratio](g:hazard-ratio) of 0.80 means a 20% lower rate of death. This is a [dose–response](g:dose-response) curve: most of the gain comes early and it levels off near 3–5× the minimum, with no sign of harm even at 10× [[c:arem-flat]].

claims.text: Compared with no leisure activity, the hazard ratio for death was 0.80 below the guideline minimum, 0.69 at 1–2 times, 0.63 at 2–3 times and 0.61 at 3–5 times.

evidence.quote: Compared with individuals reporting no leisure time physical activity, we observed a 20% lower mortality risk among those performing less than the recommended minimum of 7.5 metabolic-equivalent hours per week (HR, 0.80 [95% CI, 0.78-0.82]), a 31% lower risk at 1 to 2 times the recommended minimum (HR, 0.69 [95% CI, 0.67-0.70]), and a 37% lower risk at 2 to 3 times the minimum (HR, 0.63 [95% CI, 0.62-0.65]).

claims.text: The mortality benefit levels off at 3–5 times the minimum, and there was no evidence of harm at 10 or more times.

evidence.quote: An upper threshold for mortality benefit occurred at 3 to 5 times the physical activity recommendation (HR, 0.61 [95% CI, 0.59-0.62]); however, compared with the recommended minimum, the additional benefit was modest (31% vs 39%).
There was no evidence of harm at 10 or more times the recommended minimum (HR, 0.69 [95% CI, 0.59-0.78]).

steps.title: Measured by a device, even light movement counts
steps.text:
Questionnaires miss light movement and are often rounded up. An [accelerometer](g:accelerometer) records it. Ekelund pooled eight cohorts of wearers: 36,383 adults, mean age 62.6, median follow-up 5.8 years [[c:accel-any]]. Split into four equal groups, the death HRs from least to most active were 1.00, 0.48, 0.34 and 0.27. For light activity alone: 1.00, 0.60, 0.44, 0.38 [[c:accel-light]]; for [moderate-to-vigorous](g:mvpa) activity: 1.00, 0.64, 0.55, 0.52.

For [sedentary time](g:sedentary-behaviour) the HRs climbed: 1.00, 1.28, 1.71, 2.63 [[c:accel-sed]]. The four groups are made inside each study, so they are not minute targets.

claims.text: Any activity, at any intensity, went with lower all-cause mortality, and the pattern was non-linear.

evidence.quote: Any physical activity, regardless of intensity, was associated with lower risk of mortality, with a non-linear dose-response.

Hazards ratios for mortality were 1.00 (referent) in the first quarter (least active), 0.48 (95% confidence interval 0.43 to 0.54) in the second quarter, 0.34 (0.26 to 0.45) in the third quarter, and 0.27 (0.23 to 0.32) in the fourth quarter (most active).

claims.text: Light activity alone also went with lower mortality: HR 0.38 in the most active quarter against the least active.

evidence.quote: Corresponding hazards ratios for light physical activity were 1.00, 0.60 (0.54 to 0.68), 0.44 (0.38 to 0.51), and 0.38 (0.28 to 0.51)

claims.text: More sedentary time went with higher mortality: HR 2.63 in the most sedentary quarter against the least.

evidence.quote: For sedentary time, hazards ratios were 1.00 (referent; least sedentary), 1.28 (1.09 to 1.51), 1.71 (1.36 to 2.15), and 2.63 (1.94 to 3.56).

steps.title: Steps per day
steps.text:
Steps are easy to count. Paluch pooled 15 cohorts: 47,471 adults, 3,013 deaths, median follow-up 7.1 years. The medians of the four step groups were 3,553, 5,801, 7,842 and 10,901 steps·day⁻¹, with death HRs of 1.00, 0.60, 0.55 and 0.47 [[c:steps-hr]].

Risk kept falling until about 6,000–8,000 steps·day⁻¹ in people aged 60 and over, and 8,000–10,000 in younger adults [[c:steps-plateau]]. The paper opens by noting that the popular 10,000-step target has little evidence behind it [[c:steps-10k]].

Like every result here, this is cohort data: fitter, healthier people walk more, and illness can lower steps.

claims.text: Compared with the lowest step quartile, the death HR was 0.60, 0.55 and 0.47 in quartiles 2, 3 and 4.

evidence.quote: Compared with the lowest quartile, the adjusted HR for all-cause mortality was 0·60 (95% CI 0·51-0·71) for quartile 2, 0·55 (0·49-0·62) for quartile 3, and 0·47 (0·39-0·57) for quartile 4.

claims.text: Risk fell until about 6,000–8,000 steps a day at age 60 and over, and until 8,000–10,000 under 60.

evidence.quote: Restricted cubic splines showed progressively decreasing risk of mortality among adults aged 60 years and older with increasing number of steps per day until 6000-8000 steps per day and among adults younger than 60 years until 8000-10 000 steps per day.

claims.text: The 10,000-steps-a-day target is widely promoted but had little evidence behind it.

evidence.quote: Although 10 000 steps per day is widely promoted to have health benefits, there is little evidence to support this recommendation.

points: WHO 2020: 150–300 min moderate or 75–150 min vigorous a week (or a mix), about 450 MET-min or more, plus strength work.
MET-minutes = minutes × METs; ÷ 60 gives MET-hours. The minimum is 7.5 MET-h·week⁻¹.
Death rate falls steeply from none to a little activity and flattens near 3–5× the minimum, with no sign of harm at 10×.
Device-measured light activity counts too, and more sedentary time goes with higher risk.
Steps: risk falls until about 6,000–8,000 (60 and over) or 8,000–10,000 (younger); 10,000 is not a magic line.
All of this is observational: link, not proof of cause.

variants.stem: Under the WHO 2020 guidelines, how many minutes of vigorous aerobic activity a week is the adult target?

options.text: 75–150 min a week
options.why: Right: the vigorous range is half the moderate range, because vigorous effort counts about double.

options.text: 150–300 min a week
options.why: This is the moderate-intensity range.

options.text: 30–60 min a week
options.why: Too low: this is below the guideline minimum.

options.text: 300–450 min a week
options.why: Far above the guideline range; a high-volume week, not the target.

variants.stem: A cyclist rides 3 times a week for 60 min at 8 METs and walks 2 times for 30 min at 4 METs. What is the week's total in MET-minutes?

options.text: 1,680 MET-min
1,440 MET-min
options.why: Forgets the walks: only the rides were counted.

options.text: 240 min
options.why: Adds minutes of activity and ignores the METs: that is time, not MET-minutes.

options.text: 28 MET-min
options.why: 28 is the answer in MET-hours (1,680 ÷ 60); the unit is wrong.

variants.solution: Rides: 3 × 60 = 180 min × 8 METs = 1,440. Walks: 2 × 30 = 60 min × 4 METs = 240. Total 1,680 MET-min (28 MET-h).

variants.stem: A runner does 4 runs of 45 min at 10 METs and 1 walk of 60 min at 3 METs. What is the week's total in MET-minutes?

options.text: 1,800 MET-min
options.why: Forgets the walk.

options.text: 1,980 MET-min
240 min
options.why: Adds minutes and ignores the METs.

options.text: 33 MET-min
options.why: 33 is the MET-hours figure (1,980 ÷ 60); the unit is wrong.

variants.solution: Runs: 4 × 45 = 180 min × 10 METs = 1,800. Walk: 60 × 3 = 180. Total 1,980 MET-min (33 MET-h).

variants.stem: A triathlete swims 2 times for 30 min at 8 METs and rides once for 90 min at 6 METs. What is the week's total in MET-minutes?

options.text: 480 MET-min
options.why: Forgets the ride.

options.text: 150 min
options.why: Adds minutes and ignores the METs.

options.text: 1,020 MET-min
17 MET-min
options.why: 17 is the MET-hours figure (1,020 ÷ 60); the unit is wrong.

variants.solution: Swims: 2 × 30 = 60 min × 8 METs = 480. Ride: 90 × 6 = 540. Total 1,020 MET-min (17 MET-h).

variants.stem: Over a week a rider does 70 min of vigorous riding (6 METs) and 40 min of brisk walking (3 METs). Does this reach the 450 MET-min minimum?

options.text: Yes: 420 + 120 = 540 MET-min, above 450
options.why: Right: the mix is counted together, so neither 70 nor 40 min must reach its own range.

options.text: No: 70 vigorous min is under the 75 min minimum
options.why: Treats each intensity separately; the guideline allows an equal mix.

options.text: No: the walking is under 150 moderate min
options.why: Same error: the minimum is met by the mix, not by each intensity alone.

options.text: Yes, but only because walking counts as vigorous
options.why: Walking at 3 METs is moderate; the total is enough without changing its label.

variants.stem: Arem found a hazard ratio of 0.63 at 2–3 times the minimum, compared with no leisure activity. What does that mean?

options.text: A 63% lower rate of death
options.why: Reads the ratio as the reduction; 0.63 is what remains.

options.text: A 37% lower rate of death during follow-up
37% more years of life
options.why: A hazard ratio compares rates of death, not length of life.

options.text: 37 fewer deaths for every 100 people
options.why: It is a relative change in rate; the number of deaths depends on baseline risk.

variants.stem: In the same study, the hazard ratio below the guideline minimum was 0.80. What does that mean?

options.text: An 80% lower rate of death
options.why: Reads the ratio as the reduction; 0.80 is what remains.

options.text: 20% more years of life
options.why: A hazard ratio compares rates of death, not length of life.

options.text: A 20% lower rate of death during follow-up
20 fewer deaths for every 100 people
options.why: It is a relative change in rate, not a count of deaths.

variants.stem: At 3–5 times the minimum the hazard ratio was 0.61. What does that mean?

options.text: A 61% lower rate of death
options.why: Reads the ratio as the reduction; 0.61 is what remains.

options.text: 39% more years of life
options.why: A hazard ratio compares rates of death, not length of life.

options.text: 39 fewer deaths for every 100 people
options.why: It is a relative change in rate, not a count of deaths.

options.text: A 39% lower rate of death during follow-up

variants.stem: Person A goes from no activity to under the minimum (HR 1.00 to 0.80). Person B goes from 2–3 times the minimum to 3–5 times (HR 0.63 to 0.61). Which step shows the larger extra drop in death rate?

options.text: A: it falls 0.20, B only 0.02, so the first minutes matter most
options.why: Right: the curve is steep at the start and flat near the top.

options.text: B: more activity always brings the bigger gain
options.why: The data show the opposite: gains shrink as the dose grows.

options.text: Both are equal because each adds one dose level
options.why: Dose levels are not equal steps in effect; the HR change differs ten-fold.

options.text: B: higher doses raise risk, so it drops more
options.why: At these doses risk does not rise; the curve only flattens.

variants.stem: Person C goes from no activity to under the minimum (HR 1.00 to 0.80). Person D goes from 1–2 times (HR 0.69) to 2–3 times (HR 0.63). Which step gives the larger extra drop?

options.text: D: more minutes always bring a larger drop
options.why: The data show shrinking gains at higher doses.

options.text: C: a fall of 0.20 against D's 0.06
options.why: Right: most of the benefit comes from starting.

options.text: Equal, since each step is one band up
options.why: Each band gives a different change in HR.

options.text: D, because it starts from a lower risk
options.why: Starting lower leaves less room to fall, not more.

variants.stem: What did Arem find for people doing 10 or more times the minimum, compared with no leisure activity?

options.text: The same death rate as inactive people
options.why: The HR was 0.69, a lower rate.

options.text: A higher death rate than inactive people
options.why: The data showed no evidence of harm at this dose.

options.text: A lower death rate (HR 0.69), with no sign of extra harm
options.why: Right: the benefit stayed, though it was smaller than at 3–5 times.

options.text: The lowest death rate of all groups
options.why: The lowest rate was at 3–5 times (HR 0.61).

variants.stem: Why do accelerometer studies give a clearer picture of activity and mortality than questionnaire studies?

options.text: A device proves that activity causes longer life
options.why: A device improves measurement, not the ability to show cause.

options.text: A device records movement, including light movement that people forget or round up
options.why: Right: self-report has recall error and misses light activity.

options.text: A device removes the need to adjust for age and illness
options.why: Confounding stays; only the exposure measure is better.

options.text: A device records only vigorous exercise, which is the one that counts
options.why: Devices record all intensities; light activity also went with lower risk.

variants.stem: A 72-year-old cannot jog or ride hard, but walks slowly around the house and garden more than before. Which message fits the accelerometer data?

options.text: Light activity also went with lower mortality, so the extra movement counts
options.why: Right: HR 0.38 in the most active quarter for light activity alone.

options.text: Only moderate-to-vigorous activity counts; light movement does nothing
options.why: Light activity alone showed a clear gradient in the data.

options.text: Light activity helps only if sitting time stays the same
options.why: The study did not make this condition; both light activity and less sitting went with lower risk.

options.text: Light movement protects fully, so no harder activity is ever needed
options.why: Moderate-to-vigorous activity also went with lower risk; the data do not rank them as equal.

variants.stem: A 66-year-old averages 3,500 steps a day. Where do the pooled data say extra steps are linked to the biggest fall in risk?

options.text: Moving toward 6,000–8,000 steps a day
options.why: Right: for 60 and over, risk fell until that range.

options.text: Only after reaching 10,000 steps a day
options.why: The curve had already levelled off before 10,000 at this age.

options.text: Nowhere: steps do not change risk at this age
options.why: Risk fell clearly with more steps in this age group.

options.text: Only by walking faster at the same step count
options.why: The pooled data link total steps to risk; pace is a separate question.

variants.stem: A 38-year-old averages 11,000 steps a day. What do the pooled data suggest about adding another 2,000 steps?

options.text: A further large fall in risk, as risk always falls with steps
options.why: The curve flattens; it does not keep falling.

options.text: Little extra mortality link, since the curve flattened by 8,000–10,000
options.why: Right: beyond the plateau the data show no further fall.

options.text: An increase in risk, since 13,000 steps is excessive
options.why: The data show no rise at higher steps.

options.text: A fall only if the steps are all taken at once
options.why: The study did not test this; the finding concerns total daily steps.

variants.stem: A watch app says: you must reach 10,000 steps every day to be healthy. How should you judge this against Paluch?

options.text: It is right: risk falls until exactly 10,000 steps for all ages
options.why: The plateau came earlier for people aged 60 and over.

options.text: It is wrong: steps and death rate are not related at all
options.why: More steps clearly went with lower mortality.

options.text: It is too strict: risk levelled off at 6,000–10,000 steps, by age
options.why: Right: the data support more steps up to a range, not a sharp 10,000 line.

options.text: It is right: every step above 10,000 keeps cutting risk further
options.why: The curve flattened; extra steps added little in this data.

variants.stem: What most limits the claim that more activity lengthens life, based on cohorts like Ekelund's?

options.text: Nobody was assigned to be active, so illness and other traits may explain some of the link
options.why: Right: confounding and reverse causation remain in cohort data.

options.text: Accelerometers cannot record light activity, so the results leave it out
options.why: They record it well; light activity showed a clear link.

options.text: Meta-analyses cannot include deaths as an outcome
options.why: Deaths are a standard outcome in cohort meta-analyses.

options.text: A very large sample makes a result less reliable than a small one
options.why: Size reduces random error; it does not remove bias.
